questions.q: Why do earlier zero-trust enforcement points from this course not fully reach a SaaS application?
options: The vendor hosts the app and enforces access to it, so your own policy enforcement points have no network path to intercept traffic between a user's browser and the vendor's servers
SaaS applications are always hosted on-premises, so network controls apply automatically
SaaS applications never require any form of user authentication
Conditional access can never apply to any application outside your own data center
questions.explain: Software-defined perimeters, service mesh identity, and workload identity all assumed some control over the network path or infrastructure involved — a SaaS app breaks that assumption because the vendor hosts and governs it.

questions.q: What is 'shadow IT' and why does the lesson call it the starting point for most SaaS security programs?
options: A nickname for the IT help desk's night shift
A type of encryption used exclusively by CASB vendors
SaaS applications adopted by employees or departments without IT provisioning or visibility — you can't apply zero-trust controls to an app nobody registered
A formal, fully documented inventory of every approved SaaS application
questions.explain: Most organizations have far more SaaS tools in active use than IT has visibility into, so discovering that unmanaged layer has to happen before any policy can be applied to it.

questions.q: How does a CASB (cloud access security broker) typically enforce policy?
options: By replacing the SaaS vendor's own servers with infrastructure you control
By only scanning the SaaS tenant's configuration settings after the fact
By requiring every SaaS vendor to install a physical appliance on-premises
By inserting itself into the path between users and cloud apps, either as a proxy traffic routes through or via API integrations with the SaaS vendor
questions.explain: A CASB sits on the path between users and SaaS apps (as a proxy or via API) and from there extends DLP- and conditional-access-style controls to applications you don't host.

questions.q: What does SSPM (SaaS security posture management) check that a CASB on the traffic path would not see?
options: The volume of network traffic between a user and a SaaS app
The SaaS tenant's own configuration — things like open public sharing links, missing MFA on admin accounts, or overly permissive OAuth app grants
The physical location of the SaaS vendor's data center
Whether the user's device has enough battery life to complete a session
questions.explain: SSPM looks inward at a connected SaaS tenant's own settings and continuously flags misconfigurations and drift that a traffic-path control like a CASB would never observe, since they aren't about traffic at all.

questions.q: Why does OAuth app consent matter for zero trust, according to this lesson?
options: When an employee approves a third-party app's OAuth request, it becomes a long-lived, often invisible integration with broad access, so governing and auditing that consent is part of extending zero trust past your own infrastructure
OAuth app consent has no security implications and can be ignored
OAuth consent only ever grants read-only access and therefore needs no governance
OAuth app consent automatically expires after 24 hours in every SaaS platform
questions.explain: Clicking 'Allow' on a third-party OAuth request creates a standing integration with access to mailbox or file data that persists until explicitly revoked, which is why auditing OAuth grants is now a core part of SaaS security.
